Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
26-year-old female with new-onset dry, itchy, red rash on hands and arms for a few days after swimming; likely dermatitis.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Diffuse dry, itchy, red skin on hands and arms, onset a few days ago, noticed after swimming.  
• Associated symptoms: No spots, no cracked skin, no fever, no sweating, no vomiting, appetite and bowel/urinary function normal. Reports feeling tired; otherwise well.  
• Self-care tried: Coconut butter without benefit.  
• Past medical history: None significant; no previous eczema or dermatitis.  
• Medications: Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive pill) – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies/intolerances: Possible lactose intolerance (patient-reported). No drug allergies stated.  
• Family history: Father – asthma; Mother – hay fever; no known skin disorders.  
• Social: Lives alone; primary school teacher; non-smoker; minimal alcohol; no recreational drugs. Reports increased work stress and long hours.

Examination:
• No physical examination performed (teleconsult).  
• Vitals not recorded.

Impression:
Likely irritant or contact dermatitis of hands/arms (possible trigger: swimming pool chlorine and/or stress).

Plan:
• Provide patient information leaflet on dermatitis.  
• Topical treatment: Prescribe steroid cream (potency and regimen not documented) and regular emollient application throughout the day.  
• Symptom relief: Advise OTC oral antihistamine (e.g., chlorphenamine or loratadine) for pruritus.  
• Analgesia: Paracetamol not indicated at present.  
• Monitoring: Observe response over the next few days; if symptoms persist or worsen, return for in-person review next week.  
• Stress management discussed briefly; encourage addressing work-related stressors.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Formal allergy list confirmation; drug doses/routes/frequencies; objective skin examination and vitals; complete medication reconciliation.  
● No internal transcript conflicts noted.  
● Transcript clear; occasional minor inaudible words but clinical context preserved.
